newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African IDC to put Sasol cash back into projects. [CORRECTED 14:50 GMT]
newsitem.headline: S.African IDC to put Sasol cash back into projects. [CORRECTED 14:50 GMT]

text.p: South Africa's Industrial Development Corporation (IDC) said on Wednesday a cash windfall from a staged sale of its stake in fuels to chemicals firm Sasol Ltd would be used to fund current and new large projects.

IDC chief executive Khaya Ngqula earlier told Business Day newspaper that IDC would sell its 10 percent Sasol holding over a period of three to five years in a move that would raise about three billion (corrects from million) rand for reinvestment.
Ngqula said Sasol, set up during the apartheid era as a sanctions buster to provide the then white-run South Africa with fuel, was now a mature company.
IDC deputy managing director Jan de Bruyn told Reuters the move was a part of IDC's stated strategy to cash in its mature investments to fund the next generation of projects.
"It has always been our intention that we will sell mature investments," he said.
De Bruyn added that the cash would help fund projects already undergoing feasiblity studies as well as others that may appear in the future.
This would include the construction of steel giant Iscor Ltd's much-delayed Saldanha Steel project, which is scheduled to move into steel production in the first half of next year.
"We are busy with Saldanha still and we are looking at various other projects that will come off by the time the stake is cashed," he said.
The 6.5 billion rand Saldanha plant, which has been delayed by environmental concerns and labour unrest, is aimed at producing an initial output of 250,000 tonnes.
The IDC also has a 16 percent stake in Iscor, worth about eight billion rand, but Ngqula said the investment was not yet mature and there were no plans to sell it.

Another project that may benefit from the Sasol cash would be a planned 5.2 billion rand iron ore reduction plant pencilled in to be built either at South Africa's Phalaborwa or somewhere in Mozambique.
The plant would provide an ideal anchor client for Mozambique's Pande gas field, about 600 km north of the capital Maputo, which the Mozambican government and U.S. firm Enron Corp plan to develop.

De Bruyn declined to comment on precisely what sort of new projects could benefit from the cash, but said they were likely to be fairly large. "Though they will perhaps not be quite as big as ones we have done previously," he added.
Sasol said it was the IDC's right to dispose of its shareholding as it saw fit.
"We have provided excellent growth for our shareholders," a spokesman said.

Sasol has been agressively adjusting to the political realities of the new post-apartheid South Africa as it seeks to position itself as a global player in the fuels and chemicals arenThe firm has recently struck a rash of alliances and joint-ventures, including ones with Dow Chemical, Norway's Statoil and talks with Qatar General Petroleum Corp.
